To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the effect of LMIs is large; (ii) the effects vary across LMIs; (iii) the effect of the LMIs varies with the state of the economy; (iv) LMIs affect both unemployment and inflation; and (v) LMIs are not a source of inflation inertia.
The effects of LMIs on business cycles are large, significant, and asymmetric.
labor market institutions have a significant impact on the dynamics of inflation and unemployment, and this effect is quantitatively important.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of LMIs in the transmission mechanism of monetary policy.
the role played by LMIs on business cycle fluctuations in the OECD area.
the role of labor market institutions in the business cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
labor markets with intermediate flexibility and intermediate wage bargaining power are the most stable ones.
the effects of LMIs depend on the specific characteristics of the country and the specific type of shock.
labor market flexibility is good for the business cycle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the role of LMIs for the business cycle has been underestimated in the literature.
labor markets are more flexible than previously thought, but that they are not completely flexible.
the effects of LMIs on macroeconomic dynamics vary widely across countries, and that a country's LMI characteristics should be taken into account when assessing its macroeconomic performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
labor market policies should be designed in order to achieve a better tradeoff between the stabilization of unemployment and inflation, rather than to reduce the unemployment rate per se.
the role of LMIs in the business cycle has been underestimated.

LMIs have an important impact on the business cycle, and this effect is not necessarily negative, as is often believed.
